pageObservations.observation: Printed1 title Acceleration of a Rigid Body, Lecture11. Branding only.
Printed2 objectives: acceleration in translating/rotating frames, inertia tensor and parallel-axis theorem. No additional technical derivation.
Printed3 outline adds COM, mass distribution in robot design and URDF. Outline only.
Printed4 rigid-body idealization fixes pairwise distances; free 3D body has3 translations plus3 rotations. Joint-connected robot links are modeled as rigid, not literally undeformable real materials.

Printed5 inverse dynamics uses prescribed q,qdot,qddot to obtain effort; forward dynamics computes motion under effort for simulation. Initial state and model remain necessary even though omitted from terse forward bullet.

Printed6 explicit difference quotient definitions for linear and angular acceleration. Differentiation frame matters; universal U shorthand maps link-origin linear acceleration and body angular acceleration. Frames are part of physical definition, not removable decorative labels.

Printed7 coincident-origin derivative transport. a=R a_rel+2 omega cross R v_rel+alpha cross Rr+omega cross(omega cross Rr). Factor2 arises from two separate differentiated velocity terms. Diagram axes coincide, so no origin-translation term here.

Printed8 displaced origins require a_BORG. Diagram offset arrow points from A origin to B origin. For fixed BQ, relative velocity and acceleration vanish, leaving origin+tangential+centripetal terms; association with prismatic versus rotational joints is an application, not exclusivity of the general formula.
Printed9 omega_AC=omega_AB+R_AB omega_BC; derivative adds alpha_AB+R_AB alpha_BC+omega_AB cross(R_AB omega_BC). Transport cross term appears once, not Coriolis factor2. Vector bases must agree.

Printed10 body mass for translation, scalar axial inertia for one axis, symmetric3x3 tensor for arbitrary axis. Off-diagonal entries explicitly NEGATIVE named products Ixy,Ixz,Iyz. Diagram r from frame origin to dv.

Printed11 diagonal integrals use squared perpendicular coordinates; named products use positive integral xy rho dV etc. Thus tensor component (xy) is minus that named product. Density and dv define dm. Basis and origin determine x,y,z.

Printed12 six independent tensor scalars depend on frame origin and orientation. Principal orientation makes products zero; diagonal entries then principal moments. Diagonalization does not itself require moving origin to COM.

Printed13 COM as mass-weighted average; uniform density makes geometric centroid appropriate. Point concentration applies to translational dynamics, not replacement of an extended body inertia by zero. All individual COM positions must share a frame.
Printed14 cuboid corner frame A; x extent w, y extent l, z extent h, positive ranges0..w etc. Ixx integrates y²+z² to m(l²+h²)/3; Iyy and Izz cyclic. Corner not COM explains denominator3.
Printed15 named product integral Ixy=integral xy rho gives +mwl/4 for the positive-octant cuboid. Iyz=mlh/4 and Izx=mhw/4. Tensor entries must take negative of these named products per page361.

Printed16 full corner tensor contains negative off-diagonal mwl/4,mhw/4,mhl/4 and positive diagonals/3. Frame origin and orientation affect entries. Structured learning claim names symmetry and positive-definiteness; for ideal degenerate bodies strict positivity needs qualification.

Printed17 parallel-axis formula I_A=I_C+m[(p·p)I3−ppᵀ] with p COM relative A; C must be at COM and axes parallel. Scalar Ixy line uses matrix-entry sign convention, unlike positive named product on page362. Shift cannot be applied between arbitrary two non-COM origins without translating through COM or extra terms.

Printed18 pC=(w,l,h)/2. Subtract corner-to-COM correction to obtain Izz=m(w²+l²)/12. Off-diagonal example explicitly substitutes −mwl/4 for I_A,xy, confirming use of matrix entries here rather than named products. Diagram C shares A orientation.
Printed19 COM cuboid tensor diagonal with coefficients m/12 times sums of perpendicular squared lengths; axes parallel to original corner axes and aligned with cuboid symmetries.

Printed20 table: solid sphere2/5mR² any diameter, thin rod1/12mL² transverse COM, solid cylinder1/2mR² longitudinal, hollow cylinder mR² longitudinal, rectangular plate m(a²+b²)/12 through center. Hollow formula requires thin-wall radius model; plate requires normal axis, not any central axis.

Printed21 distal mass reduction uses perpendicular-distance squared for joint inertia; strategic batteries/actuators/counterweights for COM, hollow/I-beam/lattice shapes and topology optimization for mass/stiffness. Stable COM across all configurations is a design claim requiring scope, not guaranteed by placement alone.

Printed22 symmetric mass design reduces off-diagonal products; motor≈load inertia optimum-efficiency wording is a simplified unqualified heuristic; gear ratio and reflected-inertia reference need definition. Agility/proximal-mass stability is task-dependent, not universal.

Printed23 symmetry plane zeros only products involving its normal coordinate. Moments positive statement requires nondegenerate extent off the axis; products signed. Trace invariant under rotation of same origin, not translation. Eigenvalues principal moments, eigenvectors axes. Inertia pendulum mentioned for practical measurement.

Printed24 actual XML link forearm, mass1.5 kg, COM xyz0 0 .15, rpy0 0 0, diagonal inertia .003 .003 .001 kg m², all three off-diagonals zero. Labels principal moments hold for this diagonal inertial frame; generic off-diagonal values require component/sign convention. CAD export recommendation is source-attributed, not validation guarantee.

Printed25 summary labels Generalised case but displayed linear acceleration omits translating-origin acceleration, valid only for coincident or nonaccelerating origins; compare physical359. Angular acceleration retains the single transport cross term. Repeated parallel-axis Ixy line uses matrix-entry sign while displayed tensor labels negative named products, preserving notation ambiguity.
Printed26 bibliography: Craig 2005 and Merzouki et al. 2013. References only, no new technical examinable claim.
Printed27 Thank You closing slide only, no new technical examinable claim.

answers.reasoning: A free rigid body has three independent translations and three local orientation coordinates. Interpoint distance constraints remove independent material-point motion, not global orientation.
Rigidity is a property within each link, not across a movable joint. Joint-relative poses can change without deforming either link.

Page356 explicitly associates inverse dynamics with required torques for prescribed motion/control and forward dynamics with motion resulting from torques/simulation. The other pairings reverse one or both mappings.
Torque alone does not specify the differential equation or its initial conditions. The robot model, current state and external effects are needed; the page356 shorthand suppresses these inputs.
Differentiating R v_B produces R a_B + ω×R v_B. Differentiating ω×R q_B adds α×r plus ω×(R v_B+ω×r), yielding a second ω×v_rel.
Body-fixed Q gives v_rel=a_rel=0. With a0=ω=0, a=α×r=(0,0,3)×(2,0,0)=(0,6,0) m/s², not centripetal or sign-reversed acceleration.

The general expression reduces algebraically when q_B is constant; a specialization cannot invalidate its parent expression. The joint labels identify common use cases, not exclusive validity domains.
Principal axes are orthogonal eigenvector directions about a specified origin, giving diagonal inertia. They do not require zero or equal principal moments or a translated origin.
The eigenvalues of diag(2,3,4) are 2,3,4 kg m². A general rotated basis creates off-diagonal entries when these unequal eigenvalues mix.

A rotation diagonalizes the tensor about its existing origin. Origin translation generally changes the tensor through parallel-axis terms, so choosing directions neither specifies nor relocates the origin.

Uniform density factors out of the COM numerator and denominator, leaving the volume-centroid integral. Outer-shape symmetry or equal average density does not constrain an arbitrary internal first mass moment.
A point at the COM retains total mass and its first moment, but its inertia about that COM is zero. A spatial body generally has nonzero COM inertia in addition to its parallel-axis contribution.
The corner-based box occupies positive-coordinate intervals, so integrals xy, xz and yz do not cancel. Centered symmetry-adapted coordinates would cancel these odd cross products.

The page367 modeling proposal explicitly imposes symmetry and positive definiteness. For a nondegenerate positive-density solid these hold; merely positive diagonal entries or trace would not ensure positive quadratic forms.

Hard constraints require an architecture or enforcement operation that actually imposes them. A finite penalty or finite empirical sample is not an exact universal guarantee, and symmetrization alone does not make eigenvalues positive.
Expand (x_C+x_c)(y_C+y_c) and use zero COM first moments: Pxy,A=Pxy,C+m x_c y_c. Since the matrix entry is -Pxy, I12,A=I12,C-m x_c y_c.

Page362 defines Ixy as the raw integral, whereas pages368–369 subtract m x_c y_c and substitute the negative corner value as a matrix entry. Distinct symbols Pxy and I12 repair this sign-convention collision.

Both the matrix components and offset outer product must use the target basis before addition. With differing axes, rotate I_C and express p consistently; translating does not perform that rotation automatically.
Each uniform interval has its midpoint mean, so the COM relative to the stated corner is (w/2,l/2,h/2). Swapping x/y extents conflicts with the defined intervals.
I_axis=∫r_perp² dm equals mR² when all mass has the same geometric distance R from that axis. A finite-thickness annulus generally samples multiple radii and needs its actual distribution.
The thin plate spans a and b in its plane. A central normal axis collects both in-plane squared distances; an in-plane central axis collects only one edge contribution.
Point-mass contributions are m r²: 2(0.6²)=0.72 and 2(0.3²)=0.18 kg m². The remaining fraction is one quarter, so the decrease is 75%, not 50%.
The visible page372 bullet names batteries, actuators and counterweights as strategically placed masses. The other plausible component categories are not the named source list.
COM is a configuration-dependent weighted average of moving link locations. Strategic placement is a design aim that must be checked across configurations, not proof of constant global COM.

The source links structural forms and topology optimization with lowering mass while maintaining needed stiffness. Neither unconstrained mass minimization nor stiffness maximization captures both requirements.

Mass-reflection symmetry about a coordinate plane cancels integrands odd in its normal coordinate. COM location alone or symmetric outer geometry without matching density cannot guarantee these cancellations.

Comparing motor and load inertia is meaningful only when referred to the same generalized drive coordinate. The slide suggests approximate matching via gears; it does not compare masses or arbitrary unreferred inertias.

The slide offers no universal loss, transmission or objective model from which an optimum efficiency theorem could follow. Its matching suggestion therefore needs those qualifications rather than proving universal energy efficiency.

The r² contribution explains why less distal inertia can aid angular acceleration for a given effort. Stability and actuator limits remain task dependent, so neither guaranteed global stability nor unlimited speed follows.
Under z→-z, xz and yz change sign and cancel paired equal masses; xy is unchanged. Thus Pxz=Pyz=0 follows, but Pxy need not vanish.

A moment is an integral of nonnegative squared perpendicular distance against nonnegative mass. It is zero when all mass is on the axis, whereas negative coordinate values cannot make the moment negative.
For a symmetric inertia tensor, diagonalizing in eigenvector directions gives eigenvalues as principal moments. Eigenvectors specify directions, not scalar moments or coordinate planes.
Page374 specifically names an inertia-pendulum example. The other methods can be physically meaningful but are not the example explicitly named on this slide.

The XML example has all off-diagonal components zero, hence its inertial axes are principal directions. Positive diagonals, a COM origin, or z translation alone does not diagonalize an arbitrary tensor.
The displayed diagonal values are 0.003,0.003,0.001 kg m². The z entry is the unique minimum; x and y share the larger value.

The visible bottom line recommends SolidWorks mass-property computation with a SolidWorks-to-URDF export plugin. This is a source-attributed workflow, not a present-day software availability assertion.
The full separated-origin expression on359 has a0 plus the rotated relative, Coriolis, tangential and centripetal terms. The376 summary displays the latter four but omits a0.

The omitted additive term vanishes exactly when the B-origin acceleration relative to A is zero. Setting point-relative velocity or angular velocity to zero does not by itself remove that translational-origin term.

The derivative in the fixed U basis is the forward difference in angular velocity divided by Δt in the limit. It defines angular, not linear, acceleration and has units rad/s²; reversing subtraction changes its sign.
